faq.q: How many Quebec businesses use artificial intelligence?
faq.a: According to the Institut de la statistique du Québec (2024-2025), about 12.7% of Quebec businesses use artificial intelligence — while 52% of Quebec adults already use generative AI personally (NETendances 2025). The gap between personal use and business use is one of the biggest business opportunities for SMBs right now.

faq.q: What does an SMB need in place before adopting AI?
faq.a: Three foundations: accessible data (in software or structured files, not in email), repetitive processes that are known and written down, and one person who owns the project. Without those foundations, AI amplifies the mess instead of fixing it.

faq.q: Do you need a big budget to get started with AI in an SMB?
faq.a: No. The right first project is small and pays for itself in under twelve months: one repetitive task, measured, then eliminated. A targeted automation sprint starts at around $4,500 — a far cry from six-figure “digital transformation” projects.

questions.q: Your customer, product or order data mostly lives…
options: In emails, on paper or in someone’s head
In Excel files that everyone keeps their own way
In one or more software tools (POS, CRM, accounting)

questions.q: How often is the same information retyped from one system to another?
options: All the time — it’s daily life
For a few processes only
Almost never, our systems talk to each other

questions.q: If the person “who understands the system” left tomorrow…
options: We’d be in serious trouble
We’d manage, but slowly
Everything is documented, someone else would take over

questions.q: Your repetitive processes (invoicing, orders, reports) are…
options: In people’s heads, different depending on who does them
Known, but never written down
Written down somewhere, at least the main ones

questions.q: Is anyone on the team already using ChatGPT, Claude or another AI tool at work?
options: No, and there’s some distrust
Yes, on the quiet or each on their own
Yes, openly, we share tips

questions.q: Do you know how many hours a week go to repetitive manual tasks?
options: No idea, we’ve never counted
A gut feeling, but no number
Yes, we’ve measured it at least once

questions.q: Do your important files (price lists, quotes, contracts) arrive in usable formats?
options: No — PDFs, photos, paper that has to be retyped
A mix: some clean, others to re-enter
Yes, mostly Excel/CSV or software data

questions.q: When a data-entry error slips in (price, quantity, address), we notice it…
options: When a customer or supplier tells us
During a check, sometimes weeks later
Quickly — there’s a validation step somewhere

questions.q: Who would decide on an automation or AI project at your company?
options: Nobody — it’s nobody’s file
Management, but it’s not a clear priority
It’s settled: someone owns the project

questions.q: Your budget to fix a chore that costs $10,000 a year would be…
options: Zero — no budget for that this year
A few thousand dollars if the return is proven
Whatever it takes, if it pays for itself in under a year

tiers.titre: Ready for AI — and probably already behind
tiers.verdict: Your data exists, your processes are known and someone can own the project. At this stage, every month of waiting is a chore paid for nothing: the work isn’t to “get ready”, it’s to pick the first task to eliminate and put a number on it.
gestes: Pick ONE repetitive task and put a number on it with the calculator (hours × people × hourly cost).
Start with the cleanest data you already have (POS, accounting) — not with the most exciting project.
Require a first project to pay for itself in under twelve months; otherwise, turn it down.

tiers.verdict: The potential is real, but AI would amplify the mess as much as the order: scattered data or processes that change depending on who does them will produce fragile automations. The good news: the cleanup needed is targeted, not total.
gestes: Write down ONE repetitive process, the way it’s actually done (not the way it should be done).
Bring that process’s data into ONE single place — one master file or the existing software.
Only then, automate that process. Just one. The rest will follow the same model.

tiers.verdict: Plugging AI into operations that live in email and people’s memory is like putting a new engine in a car with no wheels. Nothing serious: the foundations take weeks, not years, and every step pays off on its own — with or without AI afterwards.
gestes: Get the critical information out of people’s heads: a price list, a customer list, a procedure — into a shared file.
Count just one thing: the hours per week spent retyping information. That number will decide what comes next.
Don’t sign anything “turnkey AI” for now — in the assessment, we set the order of the foundations, free of charge.
